title: Using Transformers to Provide Teachers with Personalized Feedback on their Classroom Discourse: The TalkMoves Application
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of scaling feedback on K-12 mathematics classroom discourse so that teachers can reflect on and improve their instructional practices more efficiently than through manual observation and coding. The authors focus on “talk moves,” a set of discourse strategies associated with productive classroom discussion, equitable participation, and student learning.

The intervention is the TalkMoves application, an end-to-end system that uses automated speech recognition and transformer-based natural language processing to analyze classroom recordings and classify teacher utterances into six accountable-talk categories plus a none class. The system then generates personalized feedback dashboards for teachers, including talk-move frequencies, teacher-versus-student talk, wait time, and changes over time. The paper reports model development experiments comparing BiLSTM, attention, and transformer variants, with RoBERTa-large performing best on the test set.

The population context is K-12 mathematics classrooms in the United States. The deployed pilot version was used by 21 teachers across grades 3–12 in two midwestern school districts during the 2019–2020 academic year, with teachers recording lessons, viewing feedback, and participating in surveys and interviews. The paper concludes that transformer-based models can provide feedback approaching human reliability for this task, but it also notes important technical challenges, especially errors from automatic speech recognition on children’s speech, and the need for continued refinement of the system.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI/NLP-based automated feedback system for analyzing classroom discourse from teacher and student speech/transcripts and producing personalized instructional feedback for K-12 teachers.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies the TalkMoves application, which uses transformer-based models and automated speech recognition to classify accountable talk moves in K-12 mathematics lessons and generate feedback dashboards for teachers.

findings.finding_summary: The system automated classroom discourse analysis and feedback generation that would otherwise require highly trained human observers and hand coding of transcripts. The paper emphasizes scalability and reduced burden, but does not report a formal comparison of labor time or cost.
findings.measure: Automation/scalability of transcript coding and feedback generation
findings.sample_size: n=21 teachers (pilot use of the application); 501 transcripts for model development

findings.finding_summary: Model performance for classifying talk moves improved to F1=79.33% with ROBERTA-LARGE on the test set, compared with 65% for the prior base model and 72.26% for the BiLSTM baseline. The paper reports MCC=0.7779 for the best model, but does not report a learner outcome effect.
findings.measure: Talk-move classification performance on held-out test set

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports technical limitations that affect system performance, including severe underestimation of student talk by Amazon Transcribe and classification errors arising from noisy classroom speech and varying talk move types. It also notes that some talk-move classes had lower individual F1 scores, including 75%, 73%, and 69%.
findings.measure: Error analysis; ASR and classification limitations

quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary system-development paper with a clear empirical model evaluation and pilot deployment, but not a randomized or quasi-experimental study of teacher or student outcomes. The evidence is mostly technical/mixed-methods rather than causal educational impact.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows moderate-to-strong technical performance for discourse classification (F1 up to 79.33%), but it does not report measurable gains in teacher practice or student learning. Reported limitations and ASR errors make the practical instructional impact unclear.
